overview.title: 📖 Overview: The Boundaries of Etnan and Muktzeh
overview.subtitle: Temurah 29a–29b
overview.hebrewSource: אֵין מוּקְצֶה אָסוּר אֶלָּא עַד שֶׁיַּעַבְדוּ בּוֹ
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The Gemara grounds the mishna's category of a muktzeh (idol-set-aside) animal in a verse about safeguarding offerings 'for Me' and not another master, then debates the precise moment such an animal stops being prohibited — whether it must be actively worked, handed to idolatrous priests, or fed 'vetches of idolatry.' A parallel discussion shows why a worshipped (ne'evad) animal remains permitted for ordinary consumption, and traces a separate, doubly-derived exclusion of a tereifa from the altar. A new mishna then defines a prostitute's payment (etnan) — even a hundred lambs given as one fee are all forbidden — before the Gemara works out exactly when payment and intercourse must occur relative to each other for the prohibition to apply, and finally debates whether payment to a gentile prostitute, an unmarried Jewish woman, or one's own menstruating wife falls under this prohibition at all.

slides.title: 📜 Muktzeh: Source and Expiration
slides.subtitle: When does 'set aside for idolatry' stop applying to an animal?
rows: Rav Yitzḥak (via Rava bar Rav Adda)
It has been used for LABOR by idol-attendants
Once worked, it won't be sacrificed to the idol afterward
It has been HANDED OVER to idol-attendants for fattening
Handover alone signals it won't be sacrificed
It has been FED 'vetches of idolatry'
A more specific marker of the animal's new, permanent status
'You shall safeguard it to sacrifice TO ME' (Num. 28:2) — 'to Me,' not to another master, i.e., not for idol worship

callout.label: Abaye's clarifying challenge:
callout.text: The verse can't mean 'every offering needs careful handling' (a weak lamb would then be disqualified) — it specifically excludes offerings intended for AN IDOL, not poor treatment in general.

slides.title: 🐐 Why a Worshipped Animal Stays Edible, and the Tereifa Puzzle
slides.subtitle: Two separate derivations from the same broader passage

nodes.content: 📖 'From the well-watered pastures of ISRAEL' (Ezekiel 45:15) — offerings come only from what's permitted TO an ordinary person
💡 If muktzeh/ne'evad were ALREADY forbidden to eat, excluding them from the altar would be obvious — so the verse must mean they're actually PERMITTED to eat, yet still barred from the altar
❓ But doesn't a tereifa (forbidden to eat) also need its own separate exclusion verse — even though 'forbidden to eat' should make altar-exclusion obvious?

✅ Yes — because the extra verse teaches something NEW: even an animal that became a tereifa only AFTER being fit and consecrated (not just one born unfit) is still excluded — a genuine novelty requiring its own text

callout.label: Layered necessity:
callout.text: Even after one verse excludes a tereifa, ANOTHER source (the animal-tithe 'passes under the rod' phrase) is needed to cover a tereifa that had a period of fitness before becoming disqualified — each layer closes a different loophole.

slides.title: 💰 New Mishna: What Counts as a Prostitute's Payment
slides.subtitle: Even scale doesn't matter, but intent does

boxes.title: Straightforward Case
items: 'Here is this lamb as your fee' — even if he actually hands over 100 lambs (having agreed to just one), ALL 100 count as payment and are forbidden
The novelty: extra animals aren't treated as a separate 'gift' — they all trace back to the same forbidden payment

boxes.title: The Maidservant Case
items: 'Take this lamb, and let your maidservant sleep with my slave' — is this 'payment for services' at all?
Rabbi Meir: NOT considered etnan (no human prostitution is technically occurring between the principals)

callout.label: Underlying theme:
callout.text: The category of etnan is defined by the TRANSACTION's structure and intent, not simply by the quantity of animals or the precise participants involved.

slides.title: ⏱️ When Must Payment and Intercourse Align?
slides.subtitle: Rabbi Elazar's timing rule, and Rav Oshaya's follow-up dilemma

steps.content: 1️⃣ Baraita: if payment was given but intercourse never happened, OR intercourse happened but payment was given only much LATER (unconnected), the animal is permitted — it doesn't retroactively become 'payment'
2️⃣ Sharpened case: if he explicitly designated THIS lamb as her fee BEFORE intercourse, it IS forbidden — even if actually handed over later — since it was already earmarked

3️⃣ Rabbi Elazar's resolution for a seeming exception: if the PROSTITUTE HERSELF already sacrificed the lamb (using her prior right to it) before the encounter occurred, it's not 'payment' at all — it no longer existed as such at the critical moment

4️⃣ Rav Oshaya's follow-up: what if she only CONSECRATED it (not yet sacrificed) before the encounter — permitted, or still forbidden? Left unresolved (תֵּיקוּ), since consecration alone may or may not count as 'removing' it the same way sacrifice does

callout.label: Underlying logic:
callout.text: 'Payment' requires the animal to genuinely belong to the transaction at the moment of the forbidden act — ownership technicalities (when exactly she acquires it) matter enormously.

slides.title: ⚖️ Whose Payment Counts as Etnan?
slides.subtitle: A four-way layered dispute over scope

lines.speaker: Rav
lines.text: Payment for ANY forbidden relation (including male-male) counts as etnan — EXCEPT payment to one's own menstruating wife, since the verse specifically says 'זוֹנָה' (a prostitute), and she isn't one.

lines.speaker: Levi
lines.text: Even payment to a menstruating wife IS forbidden — the verse also says 'תּוֹעֵבָה' (abomination), a term also used for forbidden relations like this one.

lines.speaker: Abaye
lines.text: Payment to a GENTILE prostitute is forbidden (derived from 'תּוֹעֵבָה,' linked to relations where betrothal can't take effect); payment to an UNMARRIED JEWISH prostitute is PERMITTED, since betrothal CAN take effect with her.

lines.speaker: Rava
lines.text: No distinction — payment to EITHER is forbidden, derived by analogy: since intercourse with either is forbidden to a priest by a Torah prohibition, both payments share the same forbidden status.

callout.label: A key precision from Rava:
callout.text: Even for an unmarried woman, payment isn't automatically 'etnan' — the man must explicitly frame it as payment for services ('this lamb is for you'), just as certain forbidden relations require prior warning before liability applies.

summary.principle: An animal set aside for idolatry (muktzeh) loses that status once actively used or handed over for the idol's purposes, a worshipped animal remains edible though barred from the altar, and 'payment to a prostitute' (etnan) depends precisely on the transaction's timing, framing, and the legal status of the parties involved.

flowSteps.content: 📜 Muktzeh derived from 'safeguard TO ME' — ends once worked, handed over, or fed for the idol
🐐 Worshipped animals remain edible; tereifa's altar-exclusion needs two separate verse layers

columns.content: 💰 New mishna: even 100 lambs from one fee are all forbidden; framing matters (maidservant case)
⏱️ Payment must align in time and intent with the forbidden act to count as etnan

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: the etnan prohibition's scope tracks precisely where forbidden relations and betrothal-status intersect

quiz.q: According to Rav Yitzḥak (via Rava bar Rav Adda), when does an animal set aside for idol worship (muktzeh) stop being prohibited for the altar?
o: It is always prohibited, permanently
Once it has been used for labor by idol-attendants, since it presumably won't be sacrificed to the idol afterward
The moment it is first set aside
Only after it dies of old age
quiz.e: Rav Yitzḥak holds that active use of the animal for labor by idol-attendants signals it will no longer be sacrificed to the idol, ending its muktzeh status — contrasted with Rabbi Yoḥanan's differing thresholds.

quiz.q: Why does the Gemara conclude that a muktzeh or ne'evad animal must be PERMITTED for ordinary consumption, based on Ezekiel 45:15?
o: Because the verse says nothing about consumption

Because if they were already forbidden to eat, excluding them from the altar (via that same verse) would be obviously unnecessary to state — so the verse's exclusion only makes sense if they ARE permitted to eat
Because idol-worship animals are always kosher
Because the mishna states this explicitly
quiz.e: The logic is that a verse excluding these animals from sacrifice would be superfluous if they were already forbidden to eat entirely — its necessity implies they remain permitted for ordinary consumption, just barred from the altar.

quiz.q: According to the new mishna, if a man agrees to pay a prostitute one lamb but actually gives her 100 lambs, what is the status of all 100?
o: Only the first lamb is forbidden; the rest are gifts
All 100 lambs are forbidden, since they all trace back to the same payment arrangement
None are forbidden since the amount exceeds the agreement
Only 50 are forbidden
quiz.e: The mishna teaches that even excess animals beyond the agreed fee are still considered part of the same forbidden payment (etnan), not treated as a separate gift.

quiz.q: According to Rabbi Elazar, why is a lamb NOT considered a prostitute's forbidden payment (etnan) if she sacrificed it before the encounter occurred?
o: Because sacrifice always nullifies any prior status
Because at the moment the forbidden act (or payment designation) occurs, the lamb no longer exists as an available object to serve as 'payment'
Because prostitutes cannot sacrifice animals
Because the lamb becomes non-sacred once sacrificed
quiz.e: Rabbi Elazar's principle is that etnan status requires the animal to still exist as the designated payment at the critical moment; having already been sacrificed, it can no longer retroactively become 'payment.'

quiz.q: According to Rava, in the dispute over whether payment to a gentile prostitute differs from payment to an unmarried Jewish prostitute, what is his position?
o: Only the gentile prostitute's payment is forbidden
Only the Jewish prostitute's payment is forbidden
There is no distinction — payment to EITHER is forbidden, since intercourse with both is forbidden to a priest by a Torah prohibition
Neither payment is ever forbidden
quiz.e: Rava rejects Abaye's distinction (based on whether betrothal can take effect), instead deriving both cases from their shared forbidden status for priests, concluding that both types of payment are equally prohibited as etnan.
